WORKSHEET · CLASS 29 · AGES 4 YEARS

Bunny’s Growing Garden Worksheet for Age 4

Bunny’s garden day in three pictures — write 1, 2 and 3 to put planting, watering and blooming in order.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Sequencing a three-step story is the first true comprehension skill: your child decides what happens first, next and last from pictures alone. Numbering the boxes turns that thinking into marks on paper, and the draw panel invites the ending no one can predict — what Bunny plants next.

  • Sequencing a 3-step story
  • First / next / last language
  • Number writing
  • Predicting what comes next

On the sheet: Write 1, 2, and 3 to put the story in order!

The class behind it.

Teddy’s Missing Backpack Worksheet for Age 4

Teddy’s backpack is missing! Follow the room’s clues and circle the card where the backpack waits.

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Using picture clues to answer a where question is early inference: the scene shows the backpack on the hook, and the cards test whether your child can match clue to answer. Ask “how do you know?” — the pointing and explaining is the comprehension muscle.

  • Reading picture clues
  • Matching a clue to an answer
  • Explaining a decision
  • Playroom vocabulary

On the sheet: Look at the clues. Circle where Teddy should look!

Little Lion’s Feelings Worksheet for Age 4

A gift, a dropped ice cream, a popped balloon — draw lines from each story to the feeling it gives Little Lion.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Matching events to emotions teaches the heart of story comprehension: characters feel things for reasons. Your child connects each mini-story to its feeling face, then the draw panel asks for a feeling of their own — which is where the real conversations start.

  • Matching events to feelings
  • Emotion vocabulary (happy, sad, surprised)
  • Line drawing between cards
  • Talking about feelings

On the sheet: Match each story to the correct feeling!

What your child practices.

What your child practices.

Choosing the helpful action (and noticing the unhelpful one) is problem-and-solution thinking. Because every correct answer here is a KIND one, the sheet doubles as a kindness chat: ask why the other choice wouldn’t help, and let the draw panel sketch a way your child helped this week.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

A four-step routine sequence stretches the first-next-then-last chain one step further than most four-year-olds need to track — which is exactly the right stretch. Mornings are also the routine your child knows best, so the order can be checked against real life.

  • Sequencing a 4-step routine
  • Number writing 1–4
  • Time-of-day words
  • Comparing to your own morning

On the sheet: Write 1, 2, 3, and 4. to put the story in order!

Duckling’s Cause & Effect Worksheet for Age 4

A drooping flower, a muddy puddle, a sailing boat — draw lines matching what happened to why it happened.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Cause and effect is the question readers ask forever: WHY did that happen? Pairing each what with its why (sun, rain, wind) trains the habit early, with pictures instead of print. The draw panel flips it round: your child draws a what, and YOU guess the why.

  • Cause and effect matching
  • Weather vocabulary
  • Line drawing between columns
  • Asking why

On the sheet: Match what happened to why it happened!

Every story has a WHO, a WHERE and a WHAT — circle all three for Hedgehog’s apple-tree story.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

A story map is the first graphic organizer readers meet, and this sheet is the gentlest version: one question per row, three pictured choices each. Completing it gives your child the whole skeleton of a story — character, setting, event — which they can then retell aloud.

  • Identifying character, setting, event
  • Story map vocabulary
  • One answer per question
  • Retelling from a map

On the sheet: Find WHO, WHERE, and WHAT happened!

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Each row gives a small dilemma and two actions: one kind or safe, one careless. Choosing and JUSTIFYING (out loud!) is decision-making practice wrapped in a story. The road row is worth an extra beat — crossing with a grown-up is a real-life rule worth rehearsing.

  • Best-choice reasoning
  • Safety rules (roads, spills)
  • Kindness decisions
  • Explaining a choice

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Picking out just the first and last beats of a three-part story is a focused sequencing workout: the middle must be ignored on purpose, which is harder than it sounds. Engineering-minded children will happily retell every bolt of the bridge afterwards.

  • First and last in a story

  • Retelling a build story
  • Picture comparison

What your child practices.

Needs-based clues are inference with stakes a four-year-old understands: cold means coat, rain means umbrella, hungry tummy means sandwich. The two wrong items per row are pleasantly silly, which invites the best comprehension move of all — explaining WHY not.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

  • Predicting story endings
